questions.q: Which of these is a way to bring a third variable into a two-variable scatter plot?
options: Set hue= to a third column so points are colored by it
Convert the plot to a histogram
Drop the x-axis
Sort the DataFrame by index
questions.explain: Color (hue), facets (col/row), and marker size are the standard ways to encode an additional variable in a scatter plot.

questions.q: customers.pivot_table(index='region', columns='channel', values='churned', aggfunc='mean') returns what?
options: A count of customers in each region
A list of the churned customers
The average age per channel
A region-by-channel grid whose cells are churn rates
questions.explain: The mean of a 0/1 column is a rate, so each cell holds the share of that region/channel group that churned.

questions.q: The South/app cell of the heatmap shows a churn rate of 0.35 but is based on only 20 customers. What is the right takeaway?
options: It is the proven worst segment
Cells with small counts can swing widely, so treat it as a lead to test rather than a finding
Small cells are always errors and should be deleted
The heatmap colors must be wrong
questions.explain: A rate from 20 people is unstable. Checking counts (aggfunc='count') is part of reading any rate heatmap.

questions.q: Why was the filter total_spend < 1000 applied before the pair plot?
options: Pair plots cannot handle numeric columns above 1000
To remove customers who churned
The two extreme spend values would stretch every panel involving total_spend and squash the rest of the data
seaborn requires a filter on every DataFrame
questions.explain: Extreme values stretch axes so the bulk of the data is compressed. Excluding them for an exploratory view (and noting that you did) makes the other patterns visible.

questions.q: What is a confounder in this context?
options: A column with missing values
A chart type that hides data
A duplicate row
A third variable that influences both things you are comparing, such as tenure influencing both region mix and churn
questions.explain: If a third variable drives both, an apparent two-variable link can be misleading. Breaking down by the third variable checks whether the pattern survives.
